waterbodyIdentityDecision: Retain the source-named La Mesa Reservoir as a historical freshwater study locality. This review does not establish a canonical geometry, water-management boundary, current fish community, or fishing access.
question: What fish-host names, sample counts, and collection periods can be recovered from accessible historical La Mesa Reservoir papers, and which details remain unverified or contradictory?

sourceRecords.role: Primary historical host-parasitology source. It reports five fish names collected from La Mesa Reservoir in 1989-1990 and host sample sizes, but it is not a fish-community survey.
sourceRecords.citation: Lopez, N. C. (1991). Metazoan ectoparasites of some cultured fishes from Laguna Lake and vicinities. Transactions of the National Academy of Science and Technology, 13, 499-510.
sourceRecords.reviewedSections: Abstract p. 499; materials and methods p. 500; results and Table 1 pp. 501-502; discussion pp. 509-510.

localResearchCopy.storage: Ignored local raw research storage; not an app or build input.

sourceRecords.reuse: The official-hosted PDF was readable and retained locally for research, but no item-specific open license or redistribution permission was identified. Do not redistribute the PDF, table, or parasite illustrations.

sourceRecords.role: Related secondary chapter that summarizes parasite-host results for four La Mesa fish names and cites a separate 1992 La Mesa paper. It is not independent confirmation of the 1991 sample totals.
sourceRecords.citation: Lopez, N. C. (2001). Parasitic crustaceans in fishes from some Philippine lakes. In C. B. Santiago, M. L. Cuvin-Aralar, & Z. U. Basiao (Eds.), Conservation and Ecological Management of Philippine Lakes in Relation to Fisheries and Aquaculture (pp. 75-79). Southeast Asian Fisheries Development Center, PCAMRD, and BFAR.
sourceRecords.reviewedSections: Repository record and full chapter text, especially abstract and discussion of Ergasilus philippinensis host records.
sourceRecords.reuse: The repository marks the file Open Access for reading/download. No item-specific reuse license was found; its record also notes the publication remains for sale in print. No text, table, or image is redistributed here.

sourceRecords.role: Distinct primary parasite-host paper cited by the 2001 chapter. Its bibliographic citation and a limited secondary summary were verified, but the original proceedings pages were not located or reviewed.
sourceRecords.citation: Lopez, N. C. (1992). The occurrence of Ergasilus philippinensis Velasquez, 1951 on some fishes from La Mesa Reservoir. Proceedings of the Philippine Society of Parasitologists, 1990-1991, pp. 29-33. Manila, Philippines.
sourceRecords.discoverySourceReviewedSections: Lopez 2001 chapter, pp. 75-79: Ergasilus philippinensis subsection and reference list; exact original paper not retrieved.
sourceRecords.secondaryReportedFinding: The 2001 chapter attributes four fish host names to the 1992 paper (Glossogobius giurus, Therapon plumbeus, Tilapia zillii, and Oreochromis niloticus) and reports 100% parasite prevalence in T. plumbeus. The chapter supplies no fish sample denominator, collection date, station, voucher, or original methods for that 1992 result.
sourceRecords.access: Citation verified in a full-text secondary chapter; original proceedings article not found in targeted open-web searches and not retrieved. This is not direct primary-source verification.
sourceRecords.reuse: No original file or item-specific reuse terms were obtained. Do not reproduce the underlying proceedings article or infer permission from the citing chapter's repository availability.

sourceRecords.role: Abstract-only discovery lead stating that eight fish species were known in La Mesa Reservoir and one was stocked to control algae. It provides no names or dated fish checklist.
sourceRecords.citation: Abesamis, R. A., Mamaril, A. C., & Lopez, N. C. (2001). Fish in a man-made lake: what is there to eat? (Ecological studies in La Mesa Reservoir) (Abstract only). In C. B. Santiago, M. L. Cuvin-Aralar, & Z. U. Basiao (Eds.), Conservation and Ecological Management of Philippine Lakes in Relation to Fisheries and Aquaculture (p. 157). Southeast Asian Fisheries Development Center, PCAMRD, and BFAR.
sourceRecords.reviewedSections: Repository abstract-only record and one-page abstract; no underlying ecological study or eight-taxon list was obtained.
sourceRecords.reuse: The repository lists an Open Access abstract file, but no item-specific republication license was identified. Only the abstract's source-level summary is retained as a research lead.

samplingEvidence.design: The 1991 paper examines metazoan ectoparasites of fish hosts. It says La Mesa Reservoir fish were frozen after collection and examined later; it does not establish a reservoir-wide fish census, fishery catch, or whether each fish was wild, stocked, or cultured.

sourceReportedHosts.sourceReportedParasiteContext: Three fish (15.0%) carried Cleidodiscus sp.; the paper calls the fish green sea catfish.
sourceReportedHosts.identityDisposition: Hold the species identity. The source name maps nomenclaturally to Netuma thalassina, while the current Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes entry lists the accepted taxon as brackish and marine. The source's freshwater reservoir locality and host label require independent identity/source reconciliation; do not silently substitute the accepted name.

sourceReportedHosts.sourceReportedParasiteContext: Four fish were reported with Ergasilus philippinensis.
sourceReportedHosts.identityDisposition: Source name is an exact CoL XR synonym match to Glossogobius giuris; retain source spelling and historical context in research records.

sourceReportedHosts.sourceReportedParasiteContext: One fish carried Cichlidogyrus sclerosus and the other Ergasilus philippinensis.
sourceReportedHosts.identityDisposition: Exact accepted species-rank match in the pinned CoL XR service snapshot; source specimen identity was not independently re-examined.

sourceReportedHosts.sourceReportedParasiteContext: The article reports 154 of 182 fish with Ergasilus philippinensis and 17.0% with Cichlidogyrus spp.
sourceReportedHosts.identityDisposition: Exact CoL XR synonym match to Coptodon zillii; this name match does not independently re-identify the fish.

sourceReportedHosts.sourceReportedParasiteContext: All 15 fish were reported with Ergasilus philippinensis; seven also carried Diplectanum sp.
sourceReportedHosts.identityDisposition: Exact CoL XR synonym match to Leiopotherapon plumbeus; the source's method and table disagree on the end of the collection window, so the date range is unresolved.

samplingEvidence.countInterpretation: The total is the arithmetic sum of parasite-study host sample sizes. It is not reservoir abundance, fish catch, effort-standardized catch, or a current population estimate.
samplingEvidence.dateConflict: For Therapon plumbeus, the methods say April-August 1990 while Table 1 says April-October 1990. Preserve both and do not choose one without a source correction.
sourceLimits: No specimen voucher catalogue numbers or specimen-level coordinates were located in the reviewed paper.
The paper gives study-specific collection periods and sample sizes, not a complete or current fish checklist.
The 2001 SEAFDEC chapter describes four fish taxa as wild populations and cites a separate 1992 paper; do not merge those statements or counts into the 1991 sampling table.

The distinct 1992 proceedings citation was identified as a parasite-host paper. Its four host names and 100% Therapon plumbeus prevalence are known here only through the 2001 secondary chapter; the original study's dates, sample denominator, methods, and vouchers remain unavailable.
The 2001 ecological abstract says eight fish species were known, but supplies no names; the five taxa in the 1991 host study are not a complete eight-species list.

taxonomyCrosswalk.authority: GBIF v2 species matching with explicit Catalogue of Life Extended Release checklistKey 7ddf754f-d193-4cc9-b351-99906754a03b; exact match responses are nomenclatural proposals, not specimen verification.

independentNameChecks.finding: Catalog lists current name Netuma thalassina and brackish/marine habitat; this raises a source-locality/identity question for the La Mesa record.
Catalog lists Glossogobius giuris as valid.
Catalog lists Oreochromis niloticus as valid.
Catalog lists Coptodon zillii as valid.
Catalog lists Leiopotherapon plumbeus as valid and freshwater.

imageReview.visualFinding: The 1991 article's reviewed figures are parasite illustrations/micrographs rather than standalone fish photographs. The two SEAFDEC records reviewed here provide no suitable individual fish photo with an image-to-taxon attribution trail.
imageReview.decision: Do not crop parasite figures or assign generic reservoir photos to the five fish. No new species image was added; any future photo must independently meet docs/SPECIES_IMAGE_STANDARD.md for species identity, source credit, and reusable terms.

sourceSearchAudit.scope: Bounded open-web and repository search for Lopez's distinct 1992 primary paper and a named La Mesa fish checklist; a negative result does not establish that no print or restricted copy exists.

sourceSearchAudit.result: Searches surfaced the same full-text SEAFDEC 2001 parasite chapter and abstract-only La Mesa ecology record, plus the already reviewed 1991 NAST paper. No original 1992 proceedings pages or separate named eight-fish list were retrieved. The 1996 NAST La Mesa result found in the same search concerns zooplankton, not a fish checklist.
sourceSearchAudit.decision: Keep the 1992 evidence citation-only and the eight-species statement unnamed; do not infer the three missing names from the five 1991 parasite hosts.

scopeAndReuseDecision.decision: Research-only historical host-fish crosswalk and source-discovery lead; not a current La Mesa Reservoir checklist or approved public species projection.
scopeAndReuseDecision.reason: The NAST paper is historical parasite-host research with no item-specific reuse license, no specimen vouchers, no specimen coordinates, an unresolved Therapon plumbeus date conflict, and a plausible but unresolved Arius/Netuma identity concern. The supporting SEAFDEC chapter is secondary and the eight-fish ecology source is abstract-only.

nonClaims: The 234 host fish examined in the parasite study are not an estimate of abundance, fishery catch, or current population.
The five names are not a complete La Mesa Reservoir species list; a separate 2001 abstract says eight fish species were known without naming them.
The date range for Therapon plumbeus is unresolved between the article methods and Table 1.
The source-era Arius thalassinus identification is not automatically corrected by an exact synonym match; the reservoir locality and current habitat listing require review.
No source reviewed here establishes current presence, public access, catchability, diet, safe consumption, or fishing rules.
nextActions: Continue searching lawful library catalogs and open repositories for the original Lopez (1992) proceedings pages (29-33); keep its four-host summary secondary-only until the original methods, dates, denominator, and vouchers can be checked.
Find the underlying La Mesa ecological studies or an authorized full eight-species list and identify which fish was stocked, if the source resolves the identity.
Continue NCR's 17-unit and 18-water lead inventory, including river, estuary, wetland, reservoir, bay, and other inland/coastal lanes; baseline remains incomplete.
Keep all three source records and the five candidate names research-only until identity, locality, reuse, and scope checks pass.
